validity.recommendation: Keep both rows as recorded, no merge. P7450 (Kenai Beluga Pipeline / segment "Beluga Pipeline", Beluga -> Old Tyonek, 16.21 mi) and P7458 (Beluga Pipeline, Beluga -> Anchorage, 101.35 mi, 20-inch) are two real, physically and corporately distinct pipelines that happen to share the word "Beluga" and a common origin point at the Beluga area of west Cook Inlet. The name collision is a legitimate but confusing coincidence, not a data-entry duplicate, and is worth a permanent caveat note on both rows so a future researcher does not merge them on name alone.
validity.researcher_notes: Three independent lines of evidence, none of them GEM's own wiki, all converge on the same negative verdict (not a duplicate): (1) CORPORATE/REGULATORY HISTORY -- the Regulatory Commission of Alaska's public notice of September 12, 2014 (Docket No. P-14-025, aws.state.ak.us id=174074, already the sheet's Owner ref) names 'Kenai Beluga Pipeline, LLC (KBPL), Beluga Pipeline Company (Beluga), Kenai Kachemak Pipeline, LLC (KKPL), Hilcorp Alaska, LLC d/b/a Cook Inlet Gas Gathering System (CIGGS), and Hilcorp Alaska, LLC d/b/a Kenai Nikiski Pipeline (KNPL)' as FIVE separate, pre-existing, separately-certificated applicants (holding CPCN Nos. 448, 711, 668 and 689 between them) jointly petitioning to fold their certificates into one, with KBPL surviving as the operating entity under amended CPCN 668. 'Beluga Pipeline Company' (Beluga) is listed as a distinct pre-2014 CPCN holder from KBPL itself -- proof the two 'Beluga' names were never one system administratively, only commonly owned (all five were already 100% Hilcorp Alaska, LLC subsidiaries by 2014). (2) ENVIRONMENTAL-REGULATORY DESCRIPTION -- the Alaska DEC AKG320000 'Statewide Oil and Gas Pipelines' general-permit fact sheet (dec.alaska.gov/media/mxmbp1n0/akg320000_fs_vfinal.pdf, already the sheet's Fuel ref) independently and explicitly describes two separate systems under two separate headings: 'the Beluga Pipeline section of Kenai Beluga Pipeline System' -- fed by the Tyonek Production Platform and KPL/Kaloa Junction gas, matching P7450 exactly -- versus, under its own separate heading two paragraphs later, the 'Beluga Natural Gas Transmission Pipeline' a.k.a. 'Beluga Power Plant Pipeline,' built 1984, 20-inch diameter, 'owned and operated by ENSTAR Natural Gas Company,' supplying 'the Beluga Power Plant to residential and commercial customers in Anchorage' -- matching P7458's sheet values (1984, 20-inch, Beluga-to-Anchorage) exactly, including a different owner/operator (ENSTAR/APC, not Hilcorp/Harvest/KBPL). (3) ROUTE GEOMETRY -- both PIDs' routes-repo GeoJSON traces (individual-routes/gas-pipelines/P7450.geojson, P7458.geojson) share an identical starting coordinate at Beluga but diverge into completely different corridors: P7450 runs southwest, haversine length ~16.2 mi, matching the sheet's 16.21 mi; P7458 runs east to Anchorage, haversine length ~101.2 mi, matching the sheet's 101.35 mi. This is internal corroboration only (not cited as a [ref] -- geometry is out of scope for the refs leg per the sweep SOP) but it independently reproduces the same split the two textual sources describe. PHMSA's March 2022 Final Order against Harvest Alaska, LLC (CPF No. 5-2021-023-NOPV) additionally confirms P7450's own pipeline is bi-directional, fed by 'West CIGGS sources' and the 'Beluga River Unit (BRU) Compressor,' passing through 'Kaloa Junction' -- entirely consistent with the Hilcorp/Harvest Cook Inlet gathering-and-transmission network described for P7450, and never mentions Anchorage or ENSTAR. Net: no evidence anywhere that these are the same pipe entered twice, and affirmative evidence from three independent origins (a state regulator's consolidation docket, a state environmental permit fact sheet, and route geometry) that they are not.

verifications.note: PHMSA Final Order, CPF No. 5-2021-023-NOPV, issued 2022-03-28 against Harvest Alaska, LLC, describes an actively operating, actively regulated pipeline as of 2022 (inspection/testing history through 2020, ongoing PSV maintenance obligations under 49 C.F.R. Part 192, a $73,900 civil penalty payable to close the case) and states the 'Beluga Transmission Pipeline is a bi-directional pipeline' currently carrying gas from 'West CIGGS sources' and the 'Beluga River Unit (BRU) Compressor.' status_reviews.researcher_notes: Status 'operating' CONFIRMED. Newest dated evidence I could reach is PHMSA's Final Order of 2022-03-28, an enforcement action closed by penalty payment against an actively-regulated, actively-operating Cook Inlet transmission line (inspection/testing records reviewed through 2020; ongoing Part 192 compliance obligations). This sits on top of the 2014-09-12 RCA consolidation notice, which describes KBPL beginning operation of the consolidated Beluga/CIGGS/KNPL/KKPL system on 2014-11-01 and remaining the certificate holder since. No indication anywhere (PHMSA enforcement record, RCA docket, Alaska Journal of Commerce/ADN/Petroleum News coverage of Cook Inlet gas infrastructure) that this line has been idled, abandoned, or replaced. Privately-held Hilcorp/Harvest Alaska files no SEC/EIA disclosures of its own, so there is no dated annual-report-style confirmation newer than the 2022 PHMSA order to point to, but a federal pipeline-safety enforcement action closing in 2022 against a named, still-existing operator is itself strong, recent, independent evidence of continued operation. Not stale: Hilcorp/Harvest's Cook Inlet gas system is demonstrably active business (CIGGS was even re-purposed for oil transport in 2018, per a cross_row_lead below, which presupposes CIGGS -- and by extension the shared Cook Inlet gas network the Beluga Pipeline feeds -- remained a live, maintained asset through that date). WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: a newer RCA tariff filing, PHMSA enforcement action, or Cook Inlet gas-supply news item (Alaska Journal of Commerce, Alaska Beacon, Petroleum News) reporting this specific line idled or decommissioned; none found.

cross_row_leads.facts: PHMSA Final Order, CPF No. 5-2019-0026, issued 2020-02-11 against Harvest Alaska, LLC, concerns the Kenai-Nikiski Pipeline (KNPL), not the Beluga Pipeline -- text (recovered via OCR; this PDF has no extractable text layer) states 'The pipeline was constructed in 1965 and valve VF-1 was installed in 1979,' and separately discusses a missing blowdown valve ('sometime around 2012' it was removed) and inadequate line markers at public-road crossings. If P7453 (Kenai-Nikiski Pipeline) has no sourced ConstructionYear, this 1965 date plus operator Harvest Alaska, LLC are directly usable there; note the source PDF requires OCR (pdftoppm + tesseract) since pdftotext/pypdf both find no text layer despite it being a valid, unencrypted, Tagged PDF.

Alaska DNR Division of Oil & Gas 'CIGGS Pipeline' service page states: 'The CIGGS A and CIGGS LP pipeline segments were built in 1972 and originally transported natural gas. In 2018, the system was converted to transport oil as part of the CIPL Cross Inlet Pipeline Extension Project which re-routes oil from the west side of Cook Inlet to the Andeavor (Tesoro) Refinery in Nikiski which eliminates the need for the Drift River Oil Terminal.' The same page gives CIGGS A as 16-inch/21 miles (submerged Cook Inlet lands) and CIGGS LP as 10-inch/4.7 miles (Middle Ground Shoals to the Swanson River Oil Pipeline tie-in). If P7455 (Cook Inlet Gas Gathering System) still carries Fuel='Gas'/PipelineType='gathering' for a gas commodity, this 2018 conversion to OIL transport is a material, sourced status/commodity change worth checking against the current sheet values -- DEC's AKG320000 fact sheet (already cited elsewhere in this cluster) independently corroborates CIGGS's 1972 build year and diameters but frames CIGGS in its own separate 'Cook Inlet Gas Gathering System (CIGGS)' section without mentioning the 2018 oil conversion, so the two Harvest/DNR-family sources are not perfectly reconciled and P7455's researcher should read both.
